meta.descriptionEn: In late October 1948, a thick, yellow, acrid fog settled over Donora, Pennsylvania, a steel and zinc mill town on the Monongahela River. It did not lift for five days. People coughed, struggled to breathe and could barely see the road. Firefighters ran out of oxygen, doctors rushed from door to door, and the factories kept running. Why did the fog turn so dangerous? Who was to blame? And why did a company that never admitted responsibility still pay out money? This documentary follows the town through those days, hears from the people who lived through it, and examines the science of the inversion, the pollutants and the scientist who refused to stay quiet. Discover how one small town changed how America thinks about the air we breathe.

articleEn: On the night of Friday, October 29, 1948, a thick, yellow, sharp-smelling fog lay over the streets of Donora, Pennsylvania. It was so dense that the road was hard to see. Fire Chief John Volk and his assistant Russell Davis were out answering call after call, but the oxygen they carried was running out fast. Davis later said he drove with his head out of the window, hugging the curb. This was no film scene. It was a real industrial town, a small mill town on the banks of the Monongahela River.

When the toll was counted, 20 people had died, and about 6,000 of the town's 14,000 residents had suffered breathing problems. How did this fog form? Was the weather alone to blame, or did the factories play a part? Who was responsible, did anyone answer for it, and what changed in America afterward?

In this story we first get to know Donora, then see what actually happened over those five days. After that we turn to the research, the lawsuits, and the legacy that is often counted among the beginnings of the clean air movement. The story begins on Wednesday, October 27, 1948, when the fog started to form.

articleEn: Donora sits on the Monongahela River. One source places it about 24 miles southeast of Pittsburgh, while another says about 20 miles. The sources differ a little, but both agree it is close to Pittsburgh. It became a borough in 1901, and its name joins two names: William Donner and Nora Mellon. Donner was a major tin plate and steel businessman, and Nora Mellon was the wife of banker Andrew W. Mellon.

From the start, farming, coal mining, steel and wire making were important here. Today most of that industrial capacity is gone. The site of the old steel mills is now an industrial park with about 30 tenants, run by a local authority. In 1911, Donora was the third richest borough in America. The town is nicknamed 'The Home of Champions' because well-known athletes came from here, such as baseball's Stan Musial and Ken Griffey Jr.

A trolley line opened on December 15, 1901, joining First and McKean with Fifteenth Street and Meldon. In 1911 it was extended to Black Diamond so it could meet the interurban trolley running from Charleroi to Pittsburgh. There is also an area called Cement City, where 80 houses were built by pouring concrete on site, a modular method backed by Thomas Edison. These homes were built in the early twentieth century for employees of the Donora Wire and Steel Mill, and the area is now on the National Register of Historic Places. The town is tiny, with a total area of only 2.0 square miles, including river water.

Two plants matter most for this story: the Donora Zinc Works and the American Steel & Wire plant, both owned by U.S. Steel. In 1948 Donora had 14,000 residents, living in the same river valley where these plants operated. Emissions of hydrogen fluoride and sulfur dioxide were nothing new there, and according to the source they happened often. Researchers say the zinc plant's emissions had killed nearly all vegetation within a half-mile circle. So the pollution was already there. On ordinary days, though, these gases usually dispersed into the air.
So what was different in 1948? The answer lay not in the factories but in the sky, which we turn to next.

articleEn: Air normally circulates up and down and carries pollution away. In Donora in those days, that did not happen. The reason was a temperature inversion. In meteorology, an inversion is a condition in which a layer of warm air sits on top of cooler air. Normally, in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere, temperature falls as height increases, because the sun warms the ground and that warmth heats the air above it. In an inversion this order is reversed. The air near the surface is cold, with a layer of warm air above it.

That warm layer acts like a lid. The air below cannot rise, and convection, the up-and-down movement of air, stops. The result is that smog and smoke are trapped near the ground. If the lower air is moist, fog often forms under the lid as well. Cities are more prone to this, and areas ringed by hills or valleys even more so, because the terrain blocks air movement. London's Great Smog of 1952 is also considered a major example of an inversion, with estimated deaths of 10,000 to 12,000.

Donora lay in the Monongahela River valley, where the factories were already releasing gases. Now the escape route for those gases was closing. On Wednesday, October 27, 1948, fog began to form over Donora. Another source gives the period as October 26 to October 31. This was no ordinary fog. Pollution from the factories mixed into it, and a thick, yellow, sharp-smelling smog settled on the town and hung there for five days.

The gases that would normally have dispersed were now trapped under the inversion and built up. They included sulfuric acid, nitrogen dioxide, fluorine and other poisonous gases. They kept accumulating until it rained.

One note on the dates: the count of days differs slightly. One source says five days in one place and four in another. So we will say the smog covered the town roughly from Wednesday, October 27 to Sunday, October 31, until rain came. And here is the key point: the plants were not releasing pollution for the first time. The difference was that this time the air would not let it leave. Next we look at what the people of Donora began to feel as the fog thickened.

articleEn: By Thursday, October 28, the fog was no longer just a weather matter for the people of Donora. It had begun to affect their breathing. According to the source, the smog was thick, yellowish and sharp-smelling, and breathing in it was not easy. Sources say that by October 28 many residents had started coughing and showing signs of difficulty breathing. This was a town in the Monongahela River valley with about 14,000 people, and thousands of them were about to fall ill. Warm air sat above and cold air below, so the smoke could not rise and escape. The town was like a place under a lid. At first, many illnesses and deaths were put down to asthma, so the full picture of the danger was not yet clear.

Imagine a whole town wrapped in a fog that keeps getting thicker, with people wondering when it would end. The fog was so severe that driving was nearly abandoned. Those who still went out took a great risk. Among them was Russell Davis of the Fire Department. He recalled that he drove on the left side of the road with his head out of the window, and described it as steering by scraping the curb. This shows how little could be seen. When the road cannot be seen, the curb becomes the only guide.

Conditions at home were not easy either. According to sources, roughly one third to one half of the town's population fell ill from the smog. Another source says 6,000 of 14,000 people had breathing problems. Both figures point to the same large toll. In the end 20 people died, and behind each number was a home and a family. Sixty years later, The New York Times called it one of the worst air pollution disasters in American history. The effects did not last only a few days. Ten years later, mortality rates in Donora were noticeably higher than in nearby communities.

Remember that emissions of hydrogen fluoride and sulfur dioxide were frequent in Donora. The inversion made the difference this time. If the air does not move on, the gases do not move on either. They kept collecting in the same place until the rain came. The question now was how long the conditions would last. The answer was in the hands of the weather, since in the end it was rain on Sunday that ended it.

Some people had no chance to stay home. From Friday night, the Fire Chief and his assistant kept going out on calls. Their names were John Volk and Russell Davis. In the next section we look at their work in detail.

articleEn: From the night of Friday, October 29, Fire Chief John Volk and Russell Davis kept going out on calls. This continued until the night of Sunday, October 31. Their most precious resource was oxygen. The Fire Department had 800 cubic feet of it, about 23 cubic meters. But the calls were so many that the supply ran out, and more oxygen had to be found.

Where would more oxygen come from? Volk and Davis borrowed oxygen from nearby municipalities, including McKeesport, Monessen and Charleroi. In other words, one town's need drew the whole region into the effort. According to one source, Charleroi lies about 5 miles upriver from Donora, so the neighboring towns were close. The source later counted Chief Volk and Russell Davis among two heroes who emerged during the smog.

The source also contains a quotation, though the speaker is not named there: 'I didn't take any myself.' The same quotation goes on to say that each time the speaker came back to the station, he took a small shot of whiskey. This is only a historical account of the period, not advice. The real point is that two men were trying to reach people day and night.

The town's doctors were also in the field. Eight doctors of the Donora Medical Association went from house to house seeing patients. According to the source, the whole town had just eight doctors, and between one third and one half of the roughly 14,000 residents fell ill. That ratio shows the pressure they were under. Doctors even arrived at homes where the patients belonged to another doctor, because people phoned every doctor hoping for quick treatment. The calls were scattered, with each doctor receiving separate phone calls.

The fix came on Saturday, October 30, in the afternoon. Mrs. Cora Vernon, executive director of the Red Cross, arranged it. The calls to the doctors' offices began to be transferred to an emergency center set up in the town hall, so the help became better organized. By Saturday, October 30, the smog had hung over the town for about four days, and the rain had not yet come. All this happened while the smog was still present, and in such conditions organized communication matters greatly. The story also shows how important neighboring municipalities can be in a crisis, as McKeesport, Monessen and Charleroi helped.

A question arises here. While firefighters, doctors and the Red Cross were all helping people, what were the factories doing? The answer is in the next section, and it is not simple, because according to the source an important meeting had not taken place until Sunday morning.

articleEn: On Sunday morning, October 31, plant operators and town officials met for the first time, several days after the smog began. At the meeting, Donora's burgess, meaning its mayor, August Z. Chambon, asked the plants to halt operations temporarily. Plant superintendent L.J. Westhaver replied that the plants had already begun shutting down at about 6:00 that morning. Our sources do not say who made the shutdown decision, only that according to Westhaver the work began in the morning. Could the decision have been made earlier? Our available sources give no direct answer, so we will not speculate.

The town lay in the Monongahela River valley, and in such valleys air movement can be even more limited during an inversion. During this time the air held sulfuric acid, nitrogen dioxide, fluorine and other poisonous gases, and they stayed trapped until the rain. In the end it rained on Sunday, and the rain broke the weather pattern that had kept the pollution near the ground. Volk and Davis kept answering calls through Sunday night. The next morning, Monday, the plants resumed work as usual. Once the smog ended, operations went back to normal. According to one source, nearly all vegetation within a half-mile circle of the zinc plant had already died.

Now the numbers. According to one source, 20 residents died during the smog. Between one third and one half of the population fell ill, meaning thousands of people in a town of 14,000. Another source says 6,000 people suffered breathing problems. But the story does not end there. One source says that within a month another 50 residents died of breathing-related causes. Another source says that when the inversion ended, 50 more people died, among them Lukasz Musial, father of baseball star Stan Musial.

Note that the sources differ slightly on dates. One gives the smog as October 27 to 31, the other as October 26 to 31. Both agree that 20 died during the smog and that 50 more died afterward. According to one source, the event made national headlines, and the name of a small mill town reached the whole country.

Thousands in the town were affected, yet the plants were back to normal the next morning, and this is where the question of responsibility begins. Was the smog only a mistake of the weather, or did the factories play a part? In the next section we look at the researchers' findings and the court claims.

chapters.covers: Analysis of causes: researchers focusing blame on the zinc plant; Devra Davis citing autopsy fluorine levels up to 20 times normal; fluorine gas trapped by stagnant air as primary cause; Mary Amdur's research and pressure to withdraw it; Clarence Mills's December 1948 preliminary study saying thousands more could have died if the smog had lasted longer; U.S. Steel's 'act of God' claim and American Steel & Wire's 'freak weather condition' defense; the 1951 settlement of about $235,000 spread over 80 victims and the 130 suits settled for about 5% of $4.6 million claimed; higher mortality even ten years later; property value fall of nearly 10% by 1949; plants closed by 1966.

articleEn: So who was responsible? When researchers examined the event, their attention fell mostly on pollutants from the zinc plant. One sign was that the zinc plant's emissions had killed nearly all plant life within a half-mile circle. Dr. Devra Davis, director of the Center for Environmental Oncology at the University of Pittsburgh Cancer Institute, points to autopsy results. According to her, fluorine levels in the affected people were in the range described as lethal, up to 20 times above normal. Researchers conclude that fluorine gas from the zinc smelting process was trapped in the stagnant air and was the main cause of the deaths.

Around that time Mary Amdur studied the effects of the smog. Pressure was put on her to withdraw her findings, but she refused to give in and did not withdraw them. Then came the question of the courts. U.S. Steel never accepted responsibility and called the event 'an act of God,' meaning a natural disaster. Lawsuits were filed against it. In the end, a settlement was reached in 1951 in which the company paid about $235,000. The money was divided among the 80 plaintiffs, and after legal costs very little was left to them. Meanwhile, American Steel & Wire faced 130 damage suits that claimed more than 4.6 million dollars. All these suits were settled for about 5 percent of the amount sought. The company said it was ready to prove its position in court. Its position was that the smog resulted from a 'freak weather condition' that also trapped smoke from homes, railroads, steamboats and cars over the town. In short, U.S. Steel called it 'an act of God,' while American Steel & Wire blamed the weather.

But do the later figures tell the same story? Ten years after the event, mortality rates in Donora were still noticeably higher than in nearby communities. Economic loss also appeared. By 1949, a year later, the total value of most residential property had fallen by about 10 percent. Then by 1966 U.S. Steel had closed both plants. The factories that were once the town's identity became part of history.

So was there only one cause? No. The inversion trapped the air, and researchers placed the most blame on the zinc plant. But the real impact of the disaster showed up outside the courtrooms. Next we will see how the Donora tragedy became a cause for changing the air across America.

articleEn: Donora's story did not stay confined to one town. The event led to the first large-scale epidemiological investigation of an environmental health disaster in America, which examined the health effects of a major environmental disaster on a large scale. This was a new step for the country. According to a source on the Clean Air Act, after the 1948 Donora smog people began to see air pollution as a major problem and to talk about it. Several states began making laws to reduce pollution, and in Congress the question arose whether more action was needed at the federal level.

Then in 1955 came the Air Pollution Control Act. It was the first federal law, but it set aside only 3 million dollars a year for research and training, and it did not directly control sources of pollution. The money was to go to the U.S. Public Health Service for 5 years. After that came the Clean Air Act of 1963, the first federal law that allowed the government to take direct action against air pollution. It increased cooperation between states and the federal government and set aside 95 million dollars over three years for state pollution control programs. In 1960 only 6 states had air pollution programs, but by 1970 all 50 states did. According to the source, the reason was federal funding and legislation in the 1960s. Then in 1970 the new EPA was created and major amendments came. The 1970 amendments established the National Ambient Air Quality Standards. The EPA now runs the law and makes regulations under it.

Now let us go to London. In December 1952 the Great Smog struck there, lasting from December 5 to 9. Here too an inversion trapped pollution near the ground. Initial government reports gave about 4,000 deaths, but later research put the number much higher, with estimates of 10,000 to 12,000. Donora and London both taught the world a lesson.

Yet in Donora itself, the event was little discussed for years. According to one source, a historical marker was placed on the 50th anniversary in 1998. Another part of the same source says the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission placed a marker in 1995, so the year is disputed. In 2008, on the 60th anniversary, memorial events and educational programs were held for affected families, and the town began telling its story again. Then on October 20, 2008, the Donora Smog Museum opened. It is in an old shop on McKean Avenue, and its slogan is: Clean Air Started Here.

Literature and media have also kept the story alive. Berton Roueché's article 'The Fog' was published in The New Yorker in 1950 and later became part of Eleven Blue Men. Devra Davis's 2002 book When Smoke Ran Like Water begins with the same disaster. Andy McPhee's book Donora Death Fog was published in 2023, and the documentary Rumor of Blue Sky aired on WQED TV in 2009.

Today Donora's population is much smaller. In 1948 it had 14,000 people, while the 2020 census counted 4,558. The demographics section of the article gives the figure as 4,569, so the sources differ slightly. The town is far smaller than it once was.

So what does Donora teach us? That air is shared, and that when weather and pollution combine, danger can grow quickly. Sources say climate change may increase air stagnation events in hot, dry summers. And as of 2017, some American cities were still not meeting all national ambient air quality standards.
